newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Hong Kong party leader warns of confidence fall.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong party leader warns of confidence fall.

text.p: The leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, Martin Lee, warned on Thursday that a provisional legislature appointed by Beijing threatened confidence in Hong Kong's business community.
Lee said the appointed legislature of pro-Beijing personalities went against the provisions of the 1984 Sino-British hand-over agreement and gave China the power to amend laws and curtail freedom.
"The current confidence could be very short-lived," Lee told a news conference in Stockholm at the end of a 10-city tour of Europe.
"Freedom will no longer be protected by law. Business people all cherish their freedom more than anything else.
"If something goes wrong with this market in the future...the blame lies with Beijing and its puppets in Hong Kong."
Lee said his popular Democratic Party, the largest party in the territory that emerged after the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown, was in favour of Hong Kong being returned to China.
Britain is to hand back Hong Kong with its population of 6.3 million to China at midnight on June 31, 1997, after 150 years of colonial rule.
"Realistically, if Hong Kong people were to ask for independence China would never allow that to happen and no country in the world would stand up for Hong Kong," Lee said.
"We are Chinese and we don't want to remain British. We want to be reunited with China but on all the conditions contained in the Sino-British agreement."
China is moving to replace the elected Legislative Council with a provisional legislature to set laws after the hand-over -- which was not in the terms of the 1984 agreement.
China insists the changes are merely technical and will not curtail freedoms in Hong Kong.
But Lee said this change of rules was creating nervousness in Hong Kong's business community.
"Over 60 percent of (the 529) publicly quoted companies in Hong Kong...have already moved their legal domicile outside Hong Kong," Lee said.
"I know some business people who have already left Hong Kong because of the prospect of losing their freedom...Privately business people tell their friends they are worried."
Lee dismissed criticism from Hong Kong's leader-in-waiting, Tung Chee-hwa, who has accused Lee of spreading gloom overseas about the future of Hong Kong under Chinese rule.

"Is there the need to go abroad to blacken the name of Hong Kong? Is there the need for foreigners to come to Hong Kong and tell us, the Hong Kong people, what to do in the future," Tung told reporters earlier.
Lee said the situation in Hong Kong had to be made public.
"One of the purposes of my visit... is to draw the world's attention to the imminent dangers we are facing in Hong Kong," Lee said.
"When China commits any breach of the Sino-British declaration by suppressing human rights, I think the whole world should know about it.
"I believe the Chinese leaders do care about their own international image."
